name: PDF
purpose: holds a document that looks the same everywhere it is opened, whoever opens it
note: People say „ein PDF" for any document they cannot change, which is most of what the format is known for — and the reason it exists: it was made so a page would print the same on any machine

name: ODF
purpose: holds a text document in a format nobody owns, so any office program may read and write it
note: The extension says .odt for a text and .ods for a spreadsheet — one family, several endings, which is why the family has its own name

name: DOCX
purpose: holds a text document in the format Microsoft Word writes
note: The x at the end arrived in 2007 and means the file is a zipped folder of XML — the older .doc was one opaque lump, which is why old files sometimes will not open

name: HTML
purpose: holds a web page — the text together with marks saying what is a heading, a link, a picture
note: A file a person almost never has on their own machine and meets constantly all the same: every page in the browser is one, delivered rather than stored

name: JPEG
purpose: holds a photo, made smaller by throwing away detail the eye barely notices
note: Named after the committee that agreed it, not after anything in the picture — one of the abbreviations whose long form explains nothing at all

name: PNG
purpose: holds a picture without throwing anything away, and can leave parts of it transparent
note: The transparent part is why logos are PNGs and photos are JPEGs — a difference people meet without ever being told it

name: MP3
purpose: holds music or speech, made small enough to carry thousands of them
note: For a while the word meant the player rather than the format — „ein MP3" was a device you clipped to your belt

name: MP4
purpose: holds a video together with its sound
note: Not „MP3 for video", although the names invite it: MP4 is a container that holds several streams, while MP3 is one kind of sound

name: CSV
purpose: holds a table as plain text, one row per line and the columns divided by a character
note: The comma is in the name and is a semicolon in half of Europe, because the comma is already the decimal point there — the commonest reason a CSV opens as one long column

name: EPUB
purpose: holds a book whose text reflows to fit whatever it is read on
note: The difference from a PDF is the whole point: a PDF keeps the page, an EPUB keeps the text and lets the page follow the screen

name: XML
purpose: holds data together with marks naming what each piece is, in a way both a person and a program can read
note: HTML's sibling and the reason DOCX and ODF end in an x or are called Open: inside, both are folders of XML in a ZIP

name: JSON
purpose: holds data as nested lists and name-value pairs, in a form a program reads quickly and a person can still follow
note: XML's younger rival and the one that won: the same job with far less punctuation. Almost everything a browser fetches from a server today arrives as JSON

name: ZIP
purpose: holds several files in one, made smaller, and gives them back exactly as they were
note: „Zippen" became the verb for the whole idea. It is also the quiet floor under half this list: a DOCX, an ODF and an EPUB are all ZIP files with a different ending

name: GZ
purpose: makes ONE file smaller, and nothing else — no folder, no second file
note: Which is why one so often meets `.tar.gz`: the tar puts the files into one, the gz makes that one small. Two steps where ZIP does both, and the reason the ending has two parts
